extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents/applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating novelty/anticipation under 35 U.S.C. 102 (including range/genus-species issues, public use, on-sale, and related procedural responses). Covers when prior art publications, uses, sales, or generic disclosures anticipate claimed species or ranges and how applicants may rebut.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference naming a claimed species anticipates regardless of listing size
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference that clearly names the claimed species anticipates the claim no matter how many other species are additionally named (e.g., a species listed among thousands is 'described' for §102(a) purposes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prior art explicitly names the claimed compound/species, the comprehensiveness of the listing does not negate anticipation. Case examples: Ex parte A (17 USPQ2d 1716) and In re Sivaramakrishnan. Compare to genus-species analyses when the species is not explicitly named.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic formula anticipates species when species can be 'at once envisaged'
rubrics_metrics.description: A generic chemical formula will anticipate a claimed species covered by the formula when one of ordinary skill in the art is able to 'at once envisage' the specific compound from the generic teaching (i.e., can draw the structural formula or write the name of the compound).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipation from a generic teaching requires sufficiently limited/well-delineated substituent classes. Examiners may look to preferred embodiments to determine which compounds can be anticipated. In re Petering and In re Schauman illustrate that a limited set of permutations (e.g., ~20 compounds) or limited variable sites/substituents can make a generic disclosure anticipatory; broad/enumerative generic formulas covering vast/infinite species do not anticipate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific prior-art example within a claimed range anticipates the range
rubrics_metrics.description: If a prior art reference discloses a specific example that falls within a claimed numerical or compositional range, that example anticipates the claimed range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Titanium Metals Corp. v. Banner — a data point inside claimed alloy composition range anticipated the claim. This is a straightforward anticipation where the exact claimed composition is disclosed as an example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlapping or touching prior-art range anticipates only with 'sufficient specificity'
rubrics_metrics.description: When a prior art reference teaches a range that overlaps or touches the claimed range but provides no specific example within the claimed range, anticipation requires that the reference disclose the claimed range with 'sufficient specificity' (fact-dependent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination is case-by-case: narrow claimed ranges vs broad prior ranges may not be disclosed with sufficient specificity (see Atofina v. Great Lakes Chem.). Examiners must articulate reasons for anticipation and may combine 35 U.S.C. 102/103 rejections if ambiguous. The concept parallels 'clearly envisaging' a species from a generic teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior-art values very close but not overlapping do not anticipate
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art value or range that is very close to, but does not overlap or touch, the claimed range does not anticipate the claimed range under §102.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prior art does not literally disclose the claimed endpoints or an in-range example, the proper rejection is under §103 (obviousness), not §102 (anticipation). Example: Titanium Metals Corp. v. Banner (non-overlapping data point resulted in non-anticipation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations irrelevant to §102 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of secondary considerations (unexpected results, commercial success, etc.) is irrelevant to rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102 and cannot overcome a §102 rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary considerations apply to obviousness (35 U.S.C. 103) analyses, not to literal anticipation under §102. See In re Wiggins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonanalogous art or 'teaches away' arguments are inapplicable to anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments that a prior reference is nonanalogous art or teaches away from the invention are not germane to a §102 anticipation analysis; a reference that explicitly or inherently discloses every claimed limitation is anticipatory regardless of field or disparaging language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching away and analogous-art analysis are relevant to obviousness inquiries, not to whether a reference discloses every claim limitation for novelty. Cases: Twin Disc, Inc.; Celeritas Technologies Ltd. v. Rockwell Int'l; Atlas Powder Co. See also cases addressing optional ingredients and exclusions (Upsher-Smith Labs v. Pamlab).

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(a) — 'Known or used' means publicly known or used (publicly accessible)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under §102(a), 'known or used' refers to knowledge or use that is accessible to the public; secret knowledge/use is not 'known or used' unless it is accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public accessibility is a key determinant; see Carella v. Starlight Archery and MPEP §2128. A sale of a product made by a secret process can still be 'public use' if the process can be determined by examining the product.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(a) — 'In this country' limits prior art to U.S. knowledge/use
rubrics_metrics.description: For §102(a) rejections, only knowledge or use present in the United States may be relied upon; foreign-only knowledge/use cannot form the basis of a §102(a) rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior foreign disclosures do not constitute §102(a) prior art. NAFTA/URAA changes to other statutes do not alter this meaning. See In re Ekenstam.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(a) — 'By others' means any entity different from the inventive entity
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'others' in §102(a) includes any authors/inventors different from the inventive entity; even a one-person difference is sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This interpretation preserves the one-year grace period under §102(b). See In re Katz. Applies to publications and public knowledge/use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed publication establishes prima facie §102(a) case if 'by others'
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie §102(a) case exists when a printed publication authored by others describes the invention (or an obvious variant) within the relevant time frame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the applicant is a co-author, the applicant may rebut by showing the publication derives from the applicant (disclaiming affidavits, declarations). Ex parte Hirschler, In re Katz, Ex parte Kroger examples; see MPEP §2128 for what constitutes a 'printed publication.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant rebuttal of §102(a) publication via derivation/disclaiming affidavits
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant can rebut a prima facie §102(a) case by showing that the reference's disclosure was derived from the applicant (e.g., disclaiming affidavits, declarations establishing authorship/derivation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If co-authors refuse to disclaim inventorship or claim inventorship, affidavits may be insufficient. Alternatively, adding coauthors as inventors may be possible if statutory requirements are met. See In re Katz, Ex parte Kroger, In re Searles.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.131 affidavits can antedate non-statutory-bar references
rubrics_metrics.description: When a reference is not a statutory bar under §§102(b)/(c)/(d), an applicant may overcome a §102(a) rejection by submitting a 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit to antedate the reference (or a 1.132 to show derivation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits must supply necessary evidence to antedate the critical reference date. See In re Foster and MPEP §715 for evidentiary requirements and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(b) — 1-year grace period timing rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Under §102(b) the invention is barred if patented/printed/public_use/on_sale more than one year prior to the U.S. filing date. If the one-year period would end on a weekend or federal holiday, the period is extended to the next business day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The grace period is measured from the U.S. filing date. Changes to filing date rules (e.g., Express Mail deposit) do not alter applicant's right to defer to the next business day when the last date falls on a weekend/holiday. See Ex parte Olah and MPEP §706.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(b) — CIP and effective filing date implications
rubrics_metrics.description: For continuation-in-part (CIP) applications, claims not supported by the parent get the CIP filing date; any prior art with a critical date more than one year before the CIP filing date can bar the CIP claims under §102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims relying on matter added in the CIP lack the parent's earlier priority date; see Paperless Accounting v. BART (Fed. Cir.). Examiners should determine effective dates when assessing §102(b) bars.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(b) — §102(b) rejection creates a statutory bar not overcome by affidavits or foreign priority
rubrics_metrics.description: A §102(b) rejection (outside the one-year grace period) creates a statutory bar to patentability that cannot be overcome by 37 CFR 1.131 affidavits, foreign priority dates, or proof that the applicant invented the subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outside the one-year period the applicant is barred from obtaining a patent on anticipated or obvious claims. See In re Foster and MPEP discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use test under §102(b) (Invitrogen two-prong considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The public use bar arises where the purported use was (1) accessible to the public, or (2) commercially exploited. The inquiry considers experimentation evidence, nature of the activity, public access, confidentiality obligations on observers, and commercial exploitation; this is distinct from the 'ready for patenting' prong of Pfaff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial exploitation is a strong indicator of public use but not dispositive. Examiners should evaluate evidence of public access, confidentiality, and commercialization in the context of underlying policies (encourage prompt disclosure, prevent undue private exploitation, avoid removal from public domain). See Invitrogen Corp. v. Biocrest and MPEP §2133.03(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public knowledge is not equivalent to public use under §102(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere public knowledge of an invention does not constitute a §102(b) bar — §102(b) bars public use or sale, not mere knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the only evidence is public knowledge (no public use/on-sale), the proper statutory basis may be §102(a), not §102(b). See TP Labs. v. Professional Positioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality agreements and secrecy are relevant but not dispositive to public use
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence or absence of a confidentiality agreement is one factor among many in assessing public use and should be considered as part of the totality of circumstances in light of §102(b) policy goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider nature of activity, public access, and confidentiality obligations; exhibitions with controlled access may or may not be public use depending on context (Bernhardt example). Examiners must analyze facts against policy considerations underlying the public use/on-sale bars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use by third parties deriving the invention from applicant constitutes public use if unrestricted
rubrics_metrics.description: If the inventor allows another to use the invention without limitation, restriction, or obligation of secrecy, such use constitutes a public use under §102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence/absence of formal confidentiality agreements is one factor; the core question is how much control the inventor retained. Cases: In re Smith; Egbert v. Lippmann; Ex parte C illustrates commercial transactions leading to public use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use by independent third parties may be public use if it informs the public or is ascertainable by inspection
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonsecret use by an independent third party may be a 'public use' if it sufficiently informs the public of the invention or a competitor could reasonably ascertain the invention; secret use by others is not public use if inventive details remain trade secrets and are not ascertainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether the product/system on public display or sale reveals the claimed features such that a skilled person could reconstruct the invention (Gillman, Dunlop, Lockwood, W.L. Gore). Devices placing claimed features in public possession can qualify as prior art even if other proprietary aspects remain confidential.
